title: Chapter 44 — The Chart
paragraphs: If you had followed Captain Ahab down into his cabin after the squall that took place the night after that wild ratification of his purpose with the crew, you would have seen him go to a locker in the stern, bring out a large wrinkled roll of yellowish sea charts, and spread them before him on his bolted-down table. Then, sitting down before them, you would have seen him intently studying the various lines and shadings that met his eye, and with slow but steady pencil tracing additional courses over spaces that already showed a maze of such markings. At intervals he would refer to stacks of old log-books beside him, where the records of past voyages of various ships chasing the Sperm Whale were set down in faded entries.

While he worked this way, the heavy pewter lamp suspended in chains overhead rocked constantly with the ship's motion, throwing shifting gleams and shadows of lines across his wrinkled brow. It almost seemed that while he himself was marking out lines and courses on the wrinkled charts, some invisible pencil was also tracing lines and courses upon the deeply marked chart of his forehead.

But it was not this particular night that Ahab pondered over his charts alone in his cabin. Almost every night they were brought out. Almost every night some pencil marks were erased and others substituted. For with the charts of all four oceans spread before him, Ahab was threading a maze of currents and eddies, all with a view to the more certain accomplishment of that monomaniac thought of his soul.

Now, to anyone not fully acquainted with the ways of whales, it might seem an absurdly hopeless task to seek out one solitary creature in the boundless oceans of this planet. But not so to Ahab. He knew the patterns of all tides and currents. By calculating the drifting of the sperm whale's food, and by recalling the regular, established seasons for hunting him in particular latitudes, he could arrive at reasonable estimates — almost approaching certainty — about the best times for finding his prey in any given stretch of water.

So well-established is the fact of the sperm whale's regular return to given waters that many hunters believe if he could be closely observed and studied worldwide, and if the logs of every voyage of the entire whale fleet were carefully compiled, then the migrations of the sperm whale would be found as predictable as the herring shoals or the flights of swallows. On this hint, attempts have been made to construct elaborate migration charts of the sperm whale.

Since the above was written, the statement is happily confirmed by an official circular issued by Lieutenant Maury, of the National Observatory, Washington, April 16th, 1851. By that circular, it appears that precisely such a chart is being completed, and portions of it are presented in the circular. "This chart divides the ocean into districts of five degrees of latitude by five degrees of longitude; perpendicularly through each of which districts are twelve columns for the twelve months; and horizontally through each district are three lines; one to show the number of days that have been spent in each month in every district, and the two others to show the number of days in which whales, sperm or right, have been seen."

Besides, when making a passage from one feeding-ground to another, the sperm whales — guided by some infallible instinct, or rather secret intelligence from God himself — mostly swim in veins, as they are called. They continue their way along a given ocean-line with such unwavering precision that no ship ever sailed her course by any chart with one tenth of such marvelous accuracy. Though any one whale's direction may be straight as a surveyor's line, and though the path of many may run broadly parallel along the same route, yet the individual whale rarely deviates more than a few miles from its exact course. This is because the ocean highways along which they travel provide the specific feeding opportunities the whales require.

And so, not only at known times, upon well-known separate feeding-grounds, could Ahab hope to encounter his prey. Even in crossing the widest expanses of water between those grounds, he could, by his skill, so position and time himself along the way as to still have some prospect of a meeting.

There was a circumstance that at first glance seemed to undermine his delirious but still methodical scheme. But perhaps not in reality. Though the gregarious sperm whales have their regular seasons for particular grounds, you cannot generally conclude that the herds found at such-and-such a latitude this year will be identically the same as those found there last season. There are peculiar and undeniable cases in which the opposite has proven true. In general, however, this is not the rule. So, Ahab could not hope, by tracking one known whale herd in any particular season, to find Moby Dick — as some lonely hunter would search the woods for some solitary elk. The key was this: by matching the time of year to the places where sperm whales had most often been encountered, Ahab could put himself in the best possible position, narrowing the odds against him enormously.

Now, the Pequod had sailed from Nantucket at the very beginning of the Season-on-the-Line. No effort could have enabled her commander to make the great passage southward, double Cape Horn, and then run down sixty degrees of latitude to reach the equatorial Pacific in time to cruise there. Therefore he had to wait for the next season. Yet the early departure of the Pequod had perhaps been shrewdly calculated by Ahab with exactly this in mind. Because by making a wide sweep along the northern waters, spending time among the Azores, down off the Cape de Verdes, off the mouth of the Rio de la Plata, and along the Carrol Ground — a hunting area known to be productive at that time of year — and then working his way across the Indian Ocean past the Seychelles and into the full fury of the Japanese cruising ground — by following this path, Ahab could hope that in some one of these areas, at the right moment, Moby Dick might be spotted.

But granting all this, considered calmly and coolly, does it not still seem a mad idea — that in the broad boundless ocean, one solitary whale, even if encountered, could be individually recognized by his hunter, as easily as a white-bearded man in the crowded streets of Constantinople? Yes. For the distinctive snow-white brow of Moby Dick, and his snow-white hump, could not be mistaken. And haven't I marked the whale? Ahab would mutter to himself as, after poring over his charts until long after midnight, he would lean back in his swinging chair and stare at the smoldering flame in his lamp. I've marked him, and he's marked me. He's marked me, too, he thought, touching his leg. But I'll chase him around Good Hope, and around the Horn, and around the Norway Maelstrom, and around the flames of perdition before I give him up.

Often, when forced from his hammock by exhausting and intolerably vivid dreams of the night — which, feeding on his intense daytime thoughts, carried them forward amid a clash of frenzies and whirled them round and round in his blazing brain until the very throbbing of his life became unbearable agony — and when, as sometimes happened, these spiritual torments heaved his being up from its foundations, and a chasm seemed to open in him from which forked flames and lightning shot up, and fiends beckoned him to leap down among them — when this hell within him yawned beneath him, a savage cry would be heard through the ship. Then with glaring eyes, Ahab would burst from his stateroom as though escaping a bed on fire. Yet these — perhaps — were only the outward reflections of the inner turmoil, projected beyond him by the torment inside. For at such times, mad Ahab, that thinking agent that called itself "I" was unhoused. Ahab's deeper self was a thing apart. God knows, in sleep it may have been some thinking thing within, escaping from the scorching containment of the frenzied outer mind, that vaguely tried to escape from the fire by seeking the open air of the ship's deck. But all this gave no relief. The frenzy of the mind fed on those limbs. And while his own living body lay a prisoner in its own extremity, Ahab's eternal, living principle walked among the unsleeping crew. Ahab was a sleepwalker in his own body.
